title: Airport & Planes
strapline: Passports ready — this flight is now boarding.
intent: An airport is a journey with stages — check-in, security, boarding, take-off, landing — that gives children's play a clear structure to travel through.
For many children a flight is a real, big memory (a holiday, seeing family far away), and the small world lets them replay and make sense of it.
Rich vocabulary takes off here — runway, pilot, luggage, passport, boarding pass, seatbelt, arrivals.
The play is full of purposeful writing and number: tickets, passports, gate numbers, seat rows, luggage tags.
Journeys open up the world — where planes go, who we visit, how far away 'far away' is.
implementation: Build the whole journey with the children — a check-in desk, a row of chairs for the plane, a runway — so the story has somewhere to go.
Model the roles and their talk: 'Can I see your passport, please?', 'Please fasten your seatbelt for take-off.'
Take a passenger role so children run the desk, fly the plane and announce the flights.
Leave real-looking props to write on — blank passports, boarding cards, luggage tags, a departures board.
Draw in number and place: gate 3, seat 12, how many suitcases, where in the world are we flying today?
Follow children's own trips and family stories — where have you flown, who did you visit?
key_questions: Where is your plane flying to today, and who will you visit?
What do you need to show before you can get on the plane?
Who does all the different jobs to keep everyone safe?
Which gate and which seat is this passenger in?
How will your passengers know when it's time to board?

impact.text: Children act out the whole airport journey — checking in, boarding, flying, landing — with roles for pilot, steward and passenger.
Children hold in-role conversations at the desk and on the plane, asking and answering with real back-and-forth.
Children use and understand travel vocabulary — passport, runway, luggage, boarding — correctly in play.
Children 'write' passports, tickets and luggage tags and can tell you what each one says.
Children use number for a purpose — gate and seat numbers, counting suitcases and passengers.
Children talk about places far away, journeys and the people they visit, drawing on their own experiences.

enhancements: A check-in desk with a set of scales for weighing the luggage.
Blank passports, boarding passes, luggage tags and stamps to write and stamp.
A row of chairs and paper plates for a plane cabin, with a pilot's headset.
A world map or globe to choose and find destinations.
Small suitcases and bags to pack and unpack.
A departures board with gate numbers and flight times to read and change.

playing_exploring: Children step into a big real-world event and take charge of every part of it.
They pretend fluently, becoming pilot, passenger and passport officer in turn.
active_learning: Children see the journey through from check-in to landing, keeping the sequence going with intent.
creating_thinking: Children plan the trip, solve who sits where and what each traveller needs, and adapt when the story changes.
